The first time through you do the #define and the second
time through the recursion is broken because #ifndef fails.

These two grammars are mutually recursive, but then
the .hpp files don't have to be. It looks like you can
include statement_2_grammar from statement_grammar
and avoid the reverse. There's a template declaration
for statement_grammar at the very top and it only gets
used by reference.

I had a very hard time trying to get this all to compile
when broken apart into hpp, def and instantiation files.

I need to clean all this up and code review it and doc
it. Daniel and I have been meaning to sit down and do
that together, but haven't gotten to it yet.

- Bob

In our models, we generate our includes and at the top sits "#include <stan/model/model_header.hpp>". There's no benefit to compiling any of the other .hpp files. On Sunday, May 19, 2013 4:41:02 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
Ben, what are you trying to do? I'm not sure I understand what's going on. There can only be one precompiled header file in the whole build and it needs to be included first. In our models, we generate our includes and at the top sits "#include <stan/model/model_header.hpp>". There's no benefit to compiling any of the other .hpp files. That isn't how precompiled headers work.

I'm not using the precompiled header. I'm just testing whether the header can be precompiled. That is why the precompiled headers were getting sent to /dev/null.

This test is stricter than the tests under src/test/file_includes/ because 1) it automatically applies to all 533 *.hpp files under src/stan instead of just the 117 headers that are tested by the manually created .cpp files under src/test/file_includes/ and 2) precompiling entails parsing but also does a lot more things that could trigger errors. Parsing is mostly just a check for syntax errors, rather than reconciling all the macro expansion, forward declarations, and stuff like that. If you compile the tests under src/test/file_includes/ with optimization, I think the compiler will just get rid of all the code that is #included because none of it is used by EXPECT_TRUE(true). If you precompile the header, even with optimization, the compiler has to get every part of that code into an intermediate binary state so that it can be used by an arbitrary .cpp file.

If you're looking to hunt down the make error, the only thing that looks iffy is the "@$(MAKE) ..." line. You already have the dependency on $(PCH_TESTS), so I think $(MAKE) $(PCH_TESTS) will run the target again. I haven't thought through make's sweeps over the makefile, so it might already plug in the variable and try to run make again.

I got it figured out now. The primary problem was creating a target out of src/stan/%.hpp .

Ben

Cool. Can we then just get rid of the file_includes tests?

They always seemed really clunky. I was originally thinking of
only testing the files we were targeting to be used as includes,
but I think it makes sense to test all of the .hpp files.

> and 2) precompiling entails parsing but also does a lot more things that could trigger errors.
> Parsing is mostly just a check for syntax errors, rather than reconciling all the macro expansion, forward declarations,
> and stuff like that.

Right. The only issue is that for templated code, none
of that ever happens until the template is instantiated,
which doesn't happen in a lot of our .hpp files.

> If you compile the tests under src/test/file_includes/ with optimization, I think the compiler will
> just get rid of all the code that is #included because none of it is used by EXPECT_TRUE(true).

It will get processed through the preprocessor parser, but won't
get compiled and linked unless something instantiates it.

> If you precompile the
> header, even with optimization, the compiler has to get every part of that code into an intermediate binary state so
> that it can be used by an arbitrary .cpp file.

...

I don't think this is true for templates. We'd have
to have all possible instantiations of templates tested
ahead of time for that to be true.

Instantiations is probably where we'll have to go to make
the compile times faster, so we could eventually test all
the intended instantiations. These should be tested in unit
tests, but we haven't been that thorough.

- Bob

In general, rebasing (or in general history rewriting) is a good thing for several reasons --- provided that nothing has branched from the branch whose history is being rewritten. I'll put something on the wiki, but basically

http://git-scm.com/book/en/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History

covers it.

Is the reason to rebase to make it easier to use git bisect to
debug and keep our dev branch history cleaner?  That is, if
we don't rebase and merge a feature branch into develop
with commits on it that are broken, then git bisect will break
when applied to develop?

This scenario with git bisect landing on a bad commit is one reason. Having a clean revert mechanism is another. I gave an example like this to Marco:

commit A: implement feature
commit B: add tests
commit C: add documentation

In this case, if commit A later gets reverted, commits B and C (will likely) stay, in which case you have tests that refer to code that is no longer there and documentation of a feature that is no longer there. If you

git rebase -i HEAD~2

the editor will say something like

pick A: implement feature
pick B: add tests
pick C: add documentation

and you can change it to

pick A: implement feature
squash B: add tests
squash C: add documentation

in which case the result will be something like

commit ABC: implement feature, add tests, add documentation

which is better all around in addition to being clean to revert if necessary. The same could be accomplished by reverting the commit that merges the branch (this is one of the reasons why we disallow fast-forward merges) but that would be overkill if the branch also had commit DEF that was good.

> The only downside

> test-all target, so running test-all will be stricter and more comprehensive than it was before.

Once this gets added, could you add test-pch to the list
of tests that need to pass before submitting a pull request.
I think the wiki should just say it has to pass test-all. I also want to split the function_signatures tests out of test-unit and explicitly include them in test-all.

> Can you metaprogram it somehow?

The problem is that the metaprograms themselves only get executed
when a template is instantiated.

Could we add

#ifdef TEST_ME
instatantiations
#endif

to the bottom of the .hpp files and test precompile them with -DTEST_ME added?

Ben

On Monday, May 20, 2013 2:55:33 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
That's compile, not precompile.

To me, "compile" in a C++ context means, at a minimum, "create an executable file", which isn't done in this case. I could see how test-compile would be an apt description if it did something like

$(CC) -x c++-header foo.hpp
$(CC) -include foo.hpp -o foo.o foo.cpp

In other words, it is possible that foo.hpp can be precompiled, but is somehow flawed so that foo.cpp can't be compiled, although we don't know because the second step isn't done. messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: naming & scope of header "compilation" tests
parts:
I think it's easier to understand and more future proof if tests
are named after the functionality they test rather than the
way in which they test it.

So I like Daniel's suggestion to call these "test-headers".
I like this better than "test-precompile-headers" (what Ben's
doing) or "test-compile-headers" (what our old file_includes tests
did).

We can start with our existing preprocessing test and later
add compilation tests (or even better, instantiation tests).

What we did before with the file include tests is compile a file
like stan_agrad_agrad_test.cpp:

#include <stan/agrad/agrad.hpp>
#include <gtest/gtest.h>

TEST(stanAgradAgrad,parses) {
EXPECT_TRUE(true);
}

and then run it. This will at least make sure that stan/agrad/agrad.hpp
is well-formed and exists and that all the function calls inside templated
methods exist. For example, if I have this in foo.cpp:

#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
T foo() {
return bar();
}

int main() {
std::cout << "HELLO" << std::endl;
}

Then I get a compiler error because bar() isn't defined.
Everything compiles fine if I add this above the definition of foo():

std::string bar() {
return 1;
}

It even compiles fine if there's no definition, just a declaration:

std::string bar();

But then compilation fails if I add this line to main():

std::cout << foo<double>() << std::endl;

The issue is that foo()'s template parameter T can't be
instantiated with T=double without an implementation of bar()
that returns a double.

So without the instantiations we care about, all of these tests
are technically too weak. (But better than nothing of course!)

"Precompiling" a header just saves the result of an intermediate
step of the preprocessing (and parsing?) process. I've never understood
how much, but not so much as it makes much of a difference in compiling
a model (I think maybe a 10% speedup if I remember correctly).

The Wikipedia does call what the compiler does to precompile a header
"compiling":

To reduce compilation times, some compilers allow header files
to be compiled into a form that is faster for the compiler to process.
This intermediate form is known as a precompiled header, ...

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precompiled_header

But then I think the author was being paid by the use of "compil".
In particular, I don't believe precompilation instantiates anything.

Anything that we test via creating precompiled headers (whether we keep
the precompiled header or throw it away is irrelevant), could probably
be tested in the same way we tested before, by compiling a trivial unrelated
program (like gtests's TEST macro) and running it through
g++ or clang++ (whether we want to call what g++ or clang++ does
"compilation" or not).

- Bob

The key to me is the terminology, which is clearer than Wikipedia's:

The resulting PCH file contains the serialized form of the compilerï¿½s internal
representation after it has completed parsing and semantic analysis.
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

> although it may differ for clang++ than g++, but either is supported by the test-headers target. The speedup varies if
> it is used.
>
> Did you have a thought on whether it would work to add
>
> #ifdef TEST_ME
> instantiations ...
> #endif
>
> to the .hpp files and passing -DTEST_ME when we test precompile them?

Yes, that could work, but we'd need to do more than precompile them at
that point.

I'd like to stay away from #ifdef and other preprocessor directives
to the extent possible.

To speed up compilation, we really want .o files, though the downside
is that it prevents unfolding/inlining across translation units.
But we'd like to keep our C++ usable through header only operation.
The solution we've found workable is to follow the strategy laid out
in Vandevoorde and Josuttis's book (awesome, by the way --- the one thing
everyone should read about templates and metaprogramming), is to break
the code into three files, with suffixes:

.hpp header declarations
_def.hpp definitions
_inst.cpp instantiations

Then we won't even need to test the instantations because they'll be
"tested" whenver Stan's archive is compiled.

The one example we have of this layout is in src/stan/gm/grammars.
We had to do this to keep the size down for Windows.

- Bob
